Two, and here is how the product knows the difference

The application carries industry templates. A template changes vocabulary, navigation and the dashboard without changing the code underneath: a developer sees Properties, Bookings and a Relationship Manager where a general business sees Assets, Deals and an Owner. A salesperson who has to translate the software into their own job in their head will stop using it.

Real estate and construction has its own template and modules built for it. Trading and distribution runs the general template with the order-to-cash and compliance modules: the vocabulary of trading is already ordinary, and the depth sits in the modules rather than the labels. A third template, for legal practices, exists in the codebase. It is real, we do not sell into it today, and we would rather say that than count it.

Real estate and construction: the week

One to four projects, an office and a site.

  1. Enquiries, site visits and holds

    Leads from portals, hoardings, walk-ins and brokers land in one pipeline with a relationship manager and a next date. A unit is held for a named buyer against a clock, and expired holds are swept the moment the board loads — a hold that lapsed on Friday still reading as held on Monday is a flat somebody could have sold.

  2. Demands and collections

    Construction-linked payment plans raise the demand when the milestone is certified. Ageing is bucketed 0 to 30, 31 to 60, 61 to 90 and 90 plus, matching what a bank asks for when it releases a tranche, and accrued interest sits beside those buckets rather than inside them.

  3. Contractors and running account bills

    Bills of quantity, measurement, rate analysis, certification, retention and variations. A running account bill is cumulative to date and what is paid is the difference from the previous one. Getting that backwards either double-pays a contractor money already passed on, or underpays them until work stops.

  4. Land, title and approvals

    The land screen opens with what can stop a project, not what the company owns. Occupancy certificate risk is first, because without it a finished tower cannot be occupied, buyers cannot register and lenders will not disburse. A chain of title with a gap is shown as a gap, and links nobody has checked against a certified copy are counted as unverified rather than hidden behind a tick.

The compliance a developer cannot avoid

The rules the product implements, not a list of acronyms.

  • Section 17(5) blocked credit. Works contracts for immovable property are on the list of things whose GST can never be reclaimed, which is close to a developer's whole cost base. Blocked tax is a headline figure beside the claimable one, never netted off quietly.
  • Section 43B(h). Payment to a registered micro or small enterprise later than 45 days is disallowed as an expense that year, so MSME status sits on every vendor row.
  • Section 194-IA. The buyer withholds 1 percent and pays it to the government, so what reaches you is short by design. It is recorded as credit, not a shortfall somebody chases.
  • RERA interest, where the agreement rate is compared against the symmetric rate rather than assumed. The two are often different and only one survives a dispute.
  • Dated GST rate periods per code: affordable housing at one rate and a commercial tower at another, same workspace, same month.

What Ordence does not solve for a developer

The gap between what a demo shows and what a project needs is where implementations go wrong.

  • No connection to any RERA portal. Nothing is filed. The data is in a state you can file from.
  • No site engineering. No drawings, no BIM, no CAD, no labour attendance at the gate.
  • No critical-path scheduling. Milestones and certification, yes. Primavera, no.
  • No sub-registrar integration, and no polished buyer app. A portal capability exists and we will not sell it as a customer experience.

Trading and distribution: the week

Twenty to eighty people, one or more godowns, a catalogue somebody quotes from every day.

  1. Quote and order

    A quote is built against real items at real prices with GST computed rather than typed, and an accepted quote becomes an order with its lines frozen and rates pinned. Nothing on the order screen recomputes tax, because a screen that recomputes can disagree with the document the customer holds.

  2. What is late, in rupees

    The order book leads with the value overdue, not the count. Six orders overdue and 41 lakh overdue are the same six rows and completely different meetings. Completion is value-weighted, so an order with a 50 rupee line dispatched and a 50 lakh line outstanding is not half done.

  3. Stock you can actually sell

    The emphasised figure is available: on hand minus what is already promised. Four hundred bags in the shed with three hundred committed to Thursday means a hundred are sellable, and a screen that leaves that subtraction to a tired person promises the same cement twice.

  4. Dispatch, purchase and collection

    A delivery challan against specific order lines with carrier, vehicle, driver and, where needed, the e-way bill number. Over-dispatch is refused by the database itself, naming the line and the outstanding quantity, rather than by a check concurrency can beat. Then supplier bills, the input tax credit register, GSTR-2B matched, TDS, ageing, and a Tally export.

The compliance a distributor cannot avoid

A different list from a developer's, and the differences are why a general template with these modules beats a bespoke vocabulary with none of them.

  • Correct GST on every invoice: HSN or SAC, the split decided by place of supply rather than chosen by a person, rates read from dated periods. Numbering is checked too, because a series the portal truncates collides at upload.
  • GSTR-2B reconciled before filing, with the Section 16(4) deadline attached to the credit rather than a general reminder.
  • TDS on vendor payments, including what happens when a cumulative threshold is crossed mid-year and tax becomes payable on everything paid earlier. An accountant who cannot see that catch-up amount separately cannot explain the deduction to the vendor.
  • Undeposited TDS, which accrues 1.5 percent per month under Section 201(1A) in whole months, and Section 206AB vendors who attract double the ordinary rate.

What Ordence does not solve for a distributor

The ones that come up in almost every scoping conversation.

  • No e-invoicing. No IRN and no signed QR. If your turnover requires it, raise that in the first conversation, because it changes the scope.
  • No barcode scanning and no handheld workflow in the godown. Stock moves are entered on a screen.
  • No marketplace or courier integrations. Nothing pulls orders in and nothing books a shipment.
  • No manufacturing beyond a simple bill of materials and simple work orders.
  • No bank statement import, so receipt entry is manual and bank reconciliation happens outside the product.

Who Ordence is not right for

Short, and meant seriously. Every one of these has been a conversation we ended ourselves.

  • Retail with a counter. No point of sale, no cash drawer, no loyalty programme.
  • Restaurants, salons and clinics, and manufacturers needing material requirements planning or shop-floor scheduling.
  • Regulated financial services and healthcare records. We do Indian tax and land compliance, not yours.
  • Businesses across several countries, or consolidating multiple legal entities. Ordence is India-first to the point of being India-only, and that is a limit we chose.
  • Anyone under about ten people, and anyone whose procurement requires SOC 2 or ISO 27001.

Questions people actually ask

We are in neither industry. Is it worth talking?

Sometimes. The general template plus these modules fits a lot of businesses that buy, hold and sell things with GST on them. It does not fit a business whose core workflow is something we have never seen, and twenty minutes will usually tell us both which it is.

We do both — we develop, and we trade materials.

Well handled, because both templates sit on the same ledger. Projects, land and bookings on one side, orders and stock on the other, one set of books.

Tell us what your Monday looks like.

Which screen would be open at nine, and who would be shouting about what by eleven. That answers more than a feature list.
